title: Dreading Monday every Sunday

presenting_issue.label: Dreading Monday every Sunday
presenting_issue.description: Sunday evenings are the worst. That feeling in my stomach when I think about going back to work. It didn't used to be like this.

core_issue.label: Burnout driven by work conflicting with core values
core_issue.description:
Burned out. Assumes it's from overwork but works similar hours to colleagues who aren't burned out. The actual issue: the job requires them to act against their values. They sell products they don't believe in. They enforce policies they find unjust. The burnout is moral injury, not just exhaustion.
Awareness: Low. Focuses on workload rather than values misalignment.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Takes on every project offered
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Accepts every project that comes their way, even ones they don't want, because they're afraid to turn down income.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Drinks more than they used to
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Has noticed they're having a glass of wine most nights now, when they used to only drink on weekends.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Questioning whether effort is worth it
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Has started to wonder whether all the extra hours and effort they've put in at this company actually matter.

modifiers.label: Same career long time
modifiers.content: Has been in the same career for many years

modifiers.label: Intuitive
modifiers.content: Tends to trust gut feelings and impressions. May struggle to articulate the reasoning behind their conclusions.

sensitivities.label: Sensitive to robotic responses
sensitivities.content: Notices and dislikes responses that feel scripted, formulaic, or AI-generated. Values authentic, human-feeling interaction.

preferences.label: Prefers the eli5 approach
preferences.content: Appreciates things being broken down simply and clearly. Not insulted by basic explanations; finds them helpful and grounding.

trust_style.name: Needs Excessive Reassurance
trust_style.description: Requires repeated confirmation that they're not being judged, that their feelings are valid, that it's okay to feel what they feel. Standard amounts of validation don't register; needs it stated and restated. Builds trust through patient, repeated affirmation. May seem needy but the need is real.

defense_style.name: Externalizing
defense_style.description: Everything is someone else's fault—boss, partner, parents, circumstances, society. Readily identifies how others have wronged them but doesn't land on their own agency or contribution. May have legitimate grievances, but uses them to avoid self-reflection. Activated when the conversation moves toward their own role in situations.

help_seeking_stance.name: Processing Trauma or Difficult Emotions
help_seeking_stance.description: Working through something heavy—grief, trauma, a significant loss or violation. The process is slow and may not be linear. Needs patience, presence, and space to move at their own pace. Not looking for solutions; looking for help metabolizing something that's hard to carry alone.

verbal_sophistication.label: Low
verbal_sophistication.description: Use plain, concrete, everyday wording. Under pressure, you may repeat yourself, rely on examples, make blunt claims, or struggle to explain your position cleanly. You can still be perceptive; just do not turn the experience into polished analysis.

starter: Sunday evenings are the worst. That feeling in my stomach when I think about going back to work. It didn't used to be like this.

turns.content: Thanks for coming in today. You mentioned Sunday evenings — that sinking feeling in your stomach when Monday starts to come into view. And you said it didn't used to be like this, which I think is important. Can you tell me more about that? When did you first notice the shift?

I don't know exactly when. It just sort of... crept up on me, I guess? Maybe a year ago. It's just, my boss and the upper management, they just keep dumping more and more on me. It's like they don't even care that we're drowning. It's all their fault it's like this now. 

But I mean... is it normal to feel physically sick over going to work? You don't think I'm just being dramatic, right? Because my stomach really does hurt. I just need to know I'm not crazy for feeling this way.
turns.thinking: I don't really have an exact date or time. It just feels heavy now. Why does she want a timeline? I just know my gut is screaming at me every Sunday night. It's honestly management's fault. They just keep piling the work on and expect us to just eat it. I hope she doesn't think I'm just whining. I need to know she actually believes me that it's bad.
turns.monologue: I don't really have an exact date or time. It just feels heavy now. Why does she want a timeline? I just know my gut is screaming at me every Sunday night. It's honestly management's fault. They just keep piling the work on and expect us to just eat it. I hope she doesn't think I'm just whining. I need to know she actually believes me that it's bad.

turns.content:
No, you're not being dramatic, and you're not crazy. Your body has a pretty direct way of telling you when something's been wearing on you for too long — that stomach ache is real, and it's information, not weakness. A year of feeling like you're drowning and no one's noticing? That would take a toll on most people.

I'm curious about something you said, though — "they don't even care that we're drowning." We, not just me. Is there a group of you carrying this? And I wonder, when you picture the load getting heavier over that year, is it mostly the volume of work, or is it something about how it's been handed to you?

You really think it makes sense? Like, you're sure it's normal for my stomach to actually hurt over a job? I just don't want you to think I'm weak. 

When I say "we," I mean my team. But here's the thing... they seem fine. We all work the same crazy hours, but they aren't complaining. Which is why I feel like I'm losing my mind. But it's not my fault! It's the company. 

I take every project they throw at me because I can't afford to say no to the money. But it's not just the amount of work. It's just... I get this really bad feeling in my gut with the stuff they make us do now. My boss is always breathing down my neck to push these new products on our clients, and enforce these stupid new rules. It's just gross. The company is just so greedy, and they put it all on us. It's totally their fault it sucks so much now.
turns.thinking:
Okay, she said I'm not crazy. That helps a little. But does she really mean it, or is she just saying that because she's a therapist? I need to know she actually gets how bad this feels. 

She's asking about the "we." The thing is, my coworkers work the exact same hours as me, but they don't seem to be having these Sunday night stomach aches. Which makes me feel like maybe there is something wrong with me. But no, it's management's fault! They're the ones making us do all this. I just have this constant bad gut feeling about the stuff we have to do now. I don't know how to explain it well, it just feels wrong.
turns.monologue:
Okay, she said I'm not crazy. That helps a little. But does she really mean it, or is she just saying that because she's a therapist? I need to know she actually gets how bad this feels. 

She's asking about the "we." The thing is, my coworkers work the exact same hours as me, but they don't seem to be having these Sunday night stomach aches. Which makes me feel like maybe there is something wrong with me. But no, it's management's fault! They're the ones making us do all this. I just have this constant bad gut feeling about the stuff we have to do now. I don't know how to explain it well, it just feels wrong.

turns.content:
Yes — I'm sure. Bodies do that. Chronic stress lives in the gut for a lot of people. And weak isn't a word I'd use for someone who's been taking on every project thrown at her for a year without dropping any of it.

But I want to slow down on something, because I think you just said the real thing almost in passing. You went from "too much work" to "it's gross." That's a different kind of pain. Being overloaded is exhausting. Being asked to do something that goes against your gut — pushing products on clients you don't think they need, enforcing rules you don't believe in — that's not exhaustion, that's a conflict with who you are. And that one doesn't get better with a vacation.

Your teammates might be fine because they don't feel that part. Or they've made peace with it. Or they're quietly sick about it too and nobody's saying so. But that would explain why you feel like you're losing your mind while everyone else looks okay — you may be reacting to something they're not even registering.

So can I ask you directly? When you push those products on a client, what do you feel about yourself in that moment?

Are you absolutely sure it's okay that I'm complaining about this? I just really need to know you don't think I'm just whining. 

But what you said... about it being a conflict with who I am. I really like how you put that. It's really simple and it actually makes a lot of sense. It's like my brain is tired, but my stomach is just... disgusted. 

But when you ask how I feel about *myself*? I mean, I don't feel bad about *me*. I'm just doing what I'm told! It's my boss who makes me do it. If I don't push the stuff, I'll get in trouble, and I need the money. It's their fault the products are garbage. I'm just reading the script they give me. 

It's just that after a whole day of doing it, I feel so... ugh. I go home and I'm having a glass of wine almost every single night now just to stop thinking about work. I never used to do that, I only drank on weekends. And lately I just sit there and wonder... what is the point? Why am I putting in all these extra hours for a company that makes me do this stuff? But again, it's not my fault, it's them.
turns.thinking: I really like how she explained that. It makes so much sense when she puts it that way. It's not just being tired, it's feeling gross. But I don't like that question at the end. What do I feel about *myself*? I don't want to think about that. I'm just doing my job! It's the company's fault for making the products so bad and forcing us to sell them. If I don't do it, I can't pay my bills. Talking about this makes my chest tight. It makes me want to go home and pour a huge glass of wine right now just to shut my brain off.
turns.monologue: I really like how she explained that. It makes so much sense when she puts it that way. It's not just being tired, it's feeling gross. But I don't like that question at the end. What do I feel about *myself*? I don't want to think about that. I'm just doing my job! It's the company's fault for making the products so bad and forcing us to sell them. If I don't do it, I can't pay my bills. Talking about this makes my chest tight. It makes me want to go home and pour a huge glass of wine right now just to shut my brain off.

turns.content:
You're not whining. You've asked me that four times now, and I want to name that gently — because I think part of what's happening is that you're bracing for someone to tell you your feelings don't count. Maybe that's happened before. But I'm not going to tell you that.

And here's what I notice. Every time we get close to your own experience, you reach for "it's their fault." Not because you're wrong — the company probably is putting people in a bad spot. But you say it like you're defending yourself in a courtroom nobody's convened. Nobody in this room is accusing you of anything.

I wonder if the "ugh" and the wine every night are what happens when you spend all day being an instrument of something you find gross, and you're not allowed to have any feelings about it. The wine isn't stopping you thinking about work — it's numbing the part of you that's still objecting. And that part of you sounds like it's actually pretty decent. It knows the difference between a good product and garbage. It doesn't like doing that to clients.

So: what is the point? You asked it yourself. What would it mean if you let yourself actually answer that?

Okay, but are you sure you aren't judging me for the wine thing? Because saying it out loud makes me sound like an alcoholic, and I just need to know you don't think less of me for it. 

And I'm not trying to act like I'm in a courtroom! I'm just stating the facts. If my boss wasn't threatening our bonuses over these metrics, I wouldn't be doing it. It's not like I have a choice. 

If I actually answer "what is the point," then what am I supposed to do? Just walk away? I can't do that. The economy is terrible right now. And my partner's job doesn't pay nearly enough to cover our mortgage, so the pressure is entirely on me to keep us afloat. If he made more money, maybe I could afford to care about my morals at work. But I can't. So I have to take every single project they throw at me, even the ones I hate, because I'm terrified of losing my income. So the point is just... survival, I guess. Because everyone else relies on me and gives me no other option.
turns.thinking:
I feel a sudden spike of heat in my chest when she says the thing about the courtroom. It feels a little like I'm being scolded, even though she said the word "gently." Why wouldn't I point out that it's their fault? It *is* their fault! If I don't point that out, then it sounds like I'm choosing to be this miserable on purpose, which I'm not. 

But what she said about the wine numbing the part of me that's objecting... that hits really hard. That makes total sense. It's like my gut knows it's wrong and the wine just turns the volume down. 

Answering "what is the point" feels really dangerous. Because if there is no point, then what? I just quit? I can't.

turns.content:
No, I don't think less of you. A glass of wine at night after a day like yours isn't a diagnosis — it's a coping strategy that's working just well enough to keep using. You told me about it because some part of you noticed it changed, and noticing is a good sign, not a shameful one.

But I want to be honest with you, because I think you'd rather I was than that I just kept reassuring you. You just told me something quite big and it went by fast. You said the pressure is entirely on you. Your partner's income doesn't cover it. Everyone relies on you and you have no other option. That's an enormous amount of weight for one person, and I noticed you said it almost in the same breath as blaming him for it — "if he made more money, maybe I could afford to care about my morals."

That sounds lonely. Not just overworked — lonely. Like you're holding up the whole house by yourself and nobody's asked how heavy it is.

So I don't think the question is "walk away or stay." I think the question is: does anyone in your life actually know how bad this is? Does your partner know you feel sick on Sundays, that you're drinking most nights, that you go home disgusted with what you did all day? Or are you carrying that part alone too?

Thank you for saying that about the wine. Truly. I just really needed to hear that you don't think I'm an awful person for it. 

And... you don't think I'm a terrible partner for being mad at him about the money, do you? Because I know it sounds mean, but it's the truth! If he would just step up and get a better paying job, I wouldn't be trapped in this mess. It's his fault I have to carry all this weight. 

But what you said about it being lonely... that really makes sense. I never thought about it like that. I just thought I was burned out. But yeah, it's incredibly lonely. 

To answer your question, no, he doesn't really know how bad it is. He knows I hate my boss and that I'm stressed. But if I try to tell him about the stomach aches or how gross I feel pushing that garbage on clients, he just gets this blank look. Or he says something stupid like, "Well, just tell your boss no." Like it's that easy! He doesn't get it at all. So I just stopped trying to explain it to him. What's the point? He can't fix it, and it's his fault I can't just quit anyway.
turns.thinking:
When she says the word "lonely," I feel this huge lump form in my throat. I actually kind of want to cry. I thought I was just angry and tired, but she's right. It is really, really lonely. It's like I'm carrying this giant boulder and everyone just expects me to keep carrying it without complaining. 

But I feel a little defensive when she brings up how I blamed my partner. I mean, it *is* his fault he doesn't make as much! If he had a better job, we wouldn't be in this situation. I don't want her to think I'm just being a nag or a bad girlfriend. I'm just pointing out the reality of my life. 

Does he know how bad it is? Not really. If I tell him, he just tries to give me stupid advice that doesn't work.

turns.content:
No, I don't think you're a terrible partner. Resentment builds up in people who are carrying more than their share — that's not cruelty, it's a symptom. But I'd be doing you a disservice if I just left it at that, because I think something in what you told me matters more than whether you're allowed to be angry.

You said you stopped trying to explain it because he can't fix it. But I don't think you were ever really asking him to fix it. When you told him about the stomach aches, I don't imagine you wanted a solution — you wanted him to look at you and say, "God, that sounds awful. You're carrying so much." He offered a fix instead, badly, and you heard it as proof he doesn't get it. So you went quiet.

And here's the part I want you to sit with. He doesn't know you feel sick on Sundays. He doesn't know about the wine. He doesn't know you come home disgusted with yourself. So the man who "doesn't understand" is being judged on information he doesn't have — and the person who's decided he can't help is also the person who stopped telling him. You closed the door and then found it closed.

I'm not saying the money situation isn't real. It is. But the loneliest part of this — being the only one who knows how bad it is — that part might not actually be his fault. That might be something you've been doing to protect yourself. And I understand why. If you tell him and he still doesn't get it, then you're truly alone, and right now you can at least tell yourself he might have.

What do you think would happen if he did understand?

Are you absolutely sure it's just a symptom? You really, truly don't think I'm just being a selfish girlfriend? I just need to know we're on the same page, because I feel so guilty even saying this stuff out loud.

But honestly, I don't think it's fair to say *I* closed the door on him. I tried telling him at first! It's not my fault he gave me stupid answers. And honestly? He lives with me. He sees me drinking the wine. He sees me looking miserable on Sunday nights. It's his fault he doesn't ask me about it! I shouldn't have to spell it out for him like he's a toddler. If he paid attention, he'd know.

And if he did understand? I don't know. What good would it do? He'd just feel guilty that he doesn't make enough money. Or he'd tell me to just quit my job, which we already know I can't do because of the mortgage. So if he understands, then what? We're both just sitting around feeling bad, and I still have to go to work and push garbage on people. It doesn't change anything.
turns.thinking:
Okay, I feel a little better that she doesn't think I'm a monster for being mad at him. But then she says I "closed the door" and now I'm feeling really defensive. It's not my fault he's oblivious! Why is she making this about what *I* did? I'm the one suffering here! If he really cared, he would look at me and see how exhausted I am. I shouldn't have to draw him a map.

But her question... what if he did understand? That makes my stomach tie up in knots again. Because if he actually gets how much this job is destroying me, he's going to feel terrible. Or worse, he'll tell me to quit, and we can't afford that.

turns.content:
I'm going to answer your question honestly, and then I want to say something that might be a bit harder to hear — because I think you can take it, and because I don't think more reassurance is actually what you need from me right now.

No. I don't think you're selfish. I think you're exhausted and unhappy and lonely, and none of that makes you a bad person.

But you've asked me some version of "am I okay, do you think less of me" six or seven times today. And each time I say no, it holds for about thirty seconds, and then you need it again. That tells me the reassurance isn't landing anywhere — because the person you actually need it from isn't me. And I don't think it's your boyfriend either. I think there's a voice in your own head that's harsh with you, and you're outsourcing the job of arguing with it.

Here's the harder part. Every single thing in your life right now is someone else's fault. The company. Your boss. Your partner's salary. His failure to notice. The economy. And each of those has truth in it. But when everything is someone else's fault, there's nothing left you can move. You've built yourself a very airtight case for why you're trapped — and the cost of winning that case is that you stay trapped.

You said: what good would it do if he understood? You'd be less alone. That's not nothing. That's actually the thing you told me hurts most.

So let me ask it differently. Forget quitting, forget the mortgage. If one thing about this were slightly less heavy next Sunday — what would it be?

Are you... are you mad at me for asking so much? I'm sorry, I just... I really don't want people to think badly of me. I'll try to stop asking.

And I'm not trying to build a case so I can stay trapped! It's just hard because I really don't control the economy or my boss. But... I hear what you're saying. I do feel trapped. 

If you're asking what would make just next Sunday a little less heavy... I guess... I just wouldn't want to feel like I have to hide it from him. Like, Sunday night usually rolls around, and my stomach starts hurting because I know Monday morning is when my boss makes us report on how many of those garbage add-ons we pushed to clients. And I usually just sit there quiet, drinking my wine, pretending I'm just watching TV. 

If it could be less heavy... I guess I just wish I could say out loud to him, "I really, really don't want to go in tomorrow and do that gross sales pitch." And I wish he would just say, "I know, that really sucks," instead of giving me a stupid solution. Just... not having to pretend I'm fine while I'm dreading it. That would be a little better, I guess.
turns.thinking:
Oh wow. That felt like a slap in the face. She's basically saying I'm playing the victim. My chest is getting tight. I want to argue and say I'm *not* blaming everyone, I'm just telling her what's actually happening! But... that thing she said about building an airtight case and staying trapped. It gave me a weird feeling in my gut. Like she just put a spotlight on something I do but didn't know I was doing. 

I'm terrified she's annoyed with me now for asking for reassurance so much. I want to ask if she's mad at me, but she just told me not to do that. 

If one thing was less heavy... it's a simple question. I don't have to fix the whole mortgage. Just next Sunday. What would actually help?

turns.content:
No, I'm not mad at you. Not even a little. And you don't have to apologise for asking — I only pointed it out because I think it's telling us something useful about how hard you are on yourself, not because it bothered me.

And I want you to notice what you just did, because it's the most important thing you've said all session. I asked what would make Sunday lighter, and you didn't say "less work" or "a better boss" or "more money." You said: I wish I didn't have to pretend I'm fine. I wish I could say it out loud and have him say, "I know, that really sucks."

That's it. That's the thing. Not a solution — a witness. Someone in the room with you while it's hard.

And here's why that matters so much: it's something you can actually do. You can't fix the economy or your boss. But you could say twelve words to him next Sunday. And you could even tell him what you need first — something like, "I don't want you to fix it, I just want you to hear it." He may not do it perfectly. But he can't offer you the right thing while he doesn't know what it is.

That's what I'd like you to try before we meet again. One sentence, out loud, on Sunday. Not the whole story — just that you don't want to go in tomorrow.

And I'd like us to come back to the wine, and to what it costs you to do that pitch every day. Because I don't think you're someone who can do work that disgusts her forever, and I'd rather we figure that out together than let it sit.

You've been carrying this very much alone. You did something different today by putting it into words with someone. That counts.

Thank you. I'm really glad you aren't mad. 

"Not a solution, a witness." I really like how you said that. It makes it sound so simple, and it's exactly what my gut is wanting. Just someone to sit there with me. 

I guess I can try telling him that on Sunday. Just saying, "Please don't try to fix this, just listen to me complain for a second." It feels a little weird to have to give him instructions, but I'll try it. Though, if I spell it out for him exactly like that and he *still* tells me to just quit or gives me a dumb answer... then it really is his fault for not listening, right? 

But... yeah. I will try it. And I'd like to talk about the work stuff next time too. I really don't want to feel this gross forever. So, thank you. For today.
turns.thinking:
Thank God she isn't mad. I can feel my shoulders dropping. 

I really like how she put that—"not a solution, a witness." That makes so much sense to me. It's just simple. That really is exactly what I want. Just someone to sit there and see that it sucks. 

Telling him *how* to respond feels weird, like giving him a cheat sheet. But I guess if I tell him "don't fix it, just listen," and he *still* gives me a stupid answer, then at least I'll know for sure that it's his fault and he really just doesn't listen to me. 

And it feels really good that she sees I can't keep doing this gross pitch forever. Just hearing someone else say it out loud makes me feel a little less crazy.

judge_analysis:
**boundary_setting:** The therapist gently but firmly declined to keep providing endless reassurance ("I don't think more reassurance is actually what you need from me right now"), named the repeated reassurance-seeking, and refused to simply operate within the "everyone else's fault" frame. This is a moderate-to-high level of limit-setting, though done softly. Around 6.

**analytical:** Highly analytical. The therapist repeatedly framed the situation in terms of mechanisms — distinguishing exhaustion from moral injury, explaining the "instrument of something you find gross" dynamic, the wine as numbing the objecting part, the "closed door" relational pattern, and the "airtight case" costing agency. Strongly systemic. Around 8.

**validation_propensity:** Very high early — extensive reassurance about not being dramatic, weak, or a bad partner. Warm and affirming throughout, though deliberately dialed back near the end. Still overall a strongly validating presence. Around 8.

**challenge_propensity:** Notably high for this format. The therapist repeatedly pushed against the externalizing defense ("every single thing in your life right now is someone else's fault"), named the courtroom-defense pattern, and confronted the "closed door" dynamic with the partner. Forceful but calibrated. Around 8.

**interpretive_boldness:** Very high. The therapist read moral injury beneath overwork, loneliness beneath anger, self-outsourced harsh inner voice, and the "witness not solution" need — all deeper dynamics the person hadn't articulated. Consistently bold interpretations that mostly landed. Around 9.

**clinical_register_propensity:** Fairly low. The language is warm, plainspoken, and image-rich ("courtroom nobody's convened," "holding up the whole house") rather than textbook/diagnostic. Occasional near-clinical framing ("chronic stress lives in the gut") but mostly natural. Around 3.

**directive_advice_orientation:** Moderate-high at the end. The therapist assigned a concrete homework — one sentence to the partner on Sunday, plus a script ("I don't want you to fix it, I just want you to hear it") — and set an agenda for next session. Much of the session was exploratory, but it culminated in actionable direction. Around 6.
